item.title: Cashless Bangladesh promotional campaign held at Banani Kacha Bazar
item.description:
A “Cashless Bangladesh” Promotional Campaign was held on Thursday, October 1, at Banani Kacha Bazar, Dhaka, to promote digital payments and raise public awareness about Bangla QR.
Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, MP, Minister for Finance and Planning, inaugurated the program as chief guest.
Md Ahteshamul Haque Khan, managing director & CEO of Dutch-Bangla Bank, was also present at the campaign.
During the campaign, the minister made a purchase using Bangla QR through Dutch-Bangla Bank’s app.
The program was organized by Bangladesh Bank in association with Dutch-Bangla Bank.
The minister highlighted Bangla QR as a fully encrypted and secure payment platform and urged the people to support the government’s vision of building a “Cashless Bangladesh.”
He also said that all transactions through Bangla QR under this initiative would be completely free of charge.
He further said that people would no longer need to carry cash and that the payment process would be easier and faster.
As part of its commitment to supporting the Government’s “Cashless Bangladesh” vision, Dutch-Bangla Bank has been conducting a range of awareness and promotional activities across the country to encourage both customers and merchants to use Bangla QR.
Dutch-Bangla Bank remains committed to expanding digital payment adoption and contributing to the development of a more convenient, efficient, and cashless payment ecosystem in Bangladesh.

item.title: Khasru: No fee on using Bangla QR
item.description:
Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury on Thursday said transactions through Bangla QR codes will be completely free of charge as the government moves to build a cashless Bangladesh and a digital economy.
"There will be no fee or charge for transactions through Bangla QR. Any transaction made through the QR code will be completely free, with no additional cost," he said.
The minister made the remarks while inaugurating shopping through Bangla QR codes and inspecting QR-based transactions at Banani Kitchen Market in the capital.
Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said the government would bring people from all sections of society, including Fuchka vendors, rickshaw pullers and small traders, under QR code-based digital financial services.
Under the initiative, ordinary people, roadside vendors and small businesses will be able to receive payments easily through QR codes linked to accounts with any bank or service provider, he said.
"This will eliminate the need to carry cash and make transactions easier and faster," the finance minister said.
He acknowledged that some minor technical challenges or temporary problems might arise at the initial stage, but expressed confidence that those could be resolved quickly.
Cashless transactions have already proved to be convenient and secure in many developed and rapidly growing economies around the world, he said.
"Bangladesh Bank is working to make this international practice universal in Bangladesh," he added.
The finance minister also urged citizens, businesses and service providers to participate in the government initiative to build a cashless and secure economy without hesitation.

item.title: 25 jailed over arson, vandalism during Mirpur eviction drive
item.description:
A Dhaka court has sent 25 people to jail in a case filed under the Anti-Terrorism Act, 2009, over allegations of setting fire to city corporation vehicles, vandalizing a police vehicle, attacking police and obstructing a government eviction drive in Mirpur.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Md Ripon Hossain passed the order after a hearing on Thursday.
Rafiqul Islam, a sub-inspector of the prosecution department, confirmed the matter.
The accused were produced before the court by Mirpur Model police Sub-Inspector Md Shamsuddoha, the investigating officer in the case. He sought an order to keep them in jail until the investigation is completed.
Defence lawyers sought bail for the accused. The court rejected the pleas and sent them to jail.
According to the case statement, a drive to remove illegal structures from footpaths began around 10am on Wednesday in Dhaka North City Corporation’s Zone 2 in Mirpur, led by Executive Magistrate Marufa Beg Neli.
Around 11am, an excavator disconnected an electrical wire while illegal shops were being removed from a footpath beside Baitul Quddus Jame Mosque. The mosque subsequently caught fire.
The case statement said the accused and unidentified people gathered after the incident and attempted to create unrest, claiming that the magistrate had deliberately set fire to the hawkers’ shops.
Police alleged that the group set fire to two city corporation vehicles and vandalized a bus. The city corporation filed a separate case over the incident.
The case statement also said unidentified people threw bricks and stones at a Special-71 police pickup van that arrived at the scene.
The vehicle’s windshields, bonnet, doors and other parts were damaged, while the driver and police personnel were injured, according to the statement.
The accused were also alleged to have obstructed police from carrying out their duties, assaulted police personnel and damaged the government vehicle.
Police said the accused acted in coordination to disrupt law and order and create fear among people.
The investigating officer said preliminary evidence had been found linking the accused to the incident and that the investigation was still ongoing.
He also said keeping them in jail was necessary as their release on bail could hamper the investigation.

item.title: President urges journalists to uphold professionalism, public trust
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Thursday urged television journalists to perform their duties with professionalism after maintaining public trust, contribute to nation-building and protect the public interest from their respective positions.
He made the call when a delegation of Broadcast Journalists Center (BJC) paid a courtesy call on him at Bangabhaban.
During the meeting, they discussed the current state of broadcast journalism and the media in Bangladesh, the professional development of journalists, and the responsible role of the media.
Recalling the media’s active role during the long struggle for restoration of democracy, Mirza Fakhrul sought their cooperation in institutionalising democracy in the country. He expressed gratitude to journalists for standing beside the people during difficult times in the struggle.
Recalling his interactions with journalists, the President said, “I have received your companionship, support and love.” Referring to the repression and persecution of media professionals during the fascist rule, he said, “I stood by you and I will always stand by you.”
Mirza Fakhrul said Bangladesh could have progressed like developed countries if political vendetta had been replaced by democratic practices and political and economic stability had been ensured.
He also urged all concerned to avoid narrow political interests to realise the golden opportunity created to build a new Bangladesh after a prolonged struggle and bloodshed. Turning to television channels, the President said simply increasing their number will not be enough. “Their quality must also be maintained.” He stressed the need to address the problems facing the media through the Media Reform Commission.
Mirza Fakhrul also urged policymakers to look at problems from a broader perspective, with a long-term vision and foresight, and take appropriate measures to resolve them. He emphasised collective efforts to make television channels sustainable through digitalisation and self-reliance.

item.title: Bangladesh end ASEAN Cup campaign with 9-2 defeat to Indonesia
item.description:
Bangladesh concluded their inaugural FIFA ASEAN Cup campaign with a crushing 9-2 defeat to Indonesia in their final Group A match at the Gelora Bung Karno Stadium in Jakarta on Thursday.
Competing as a guest team against higher-ranked opponents after what coach Thomas Dooley described as insufficient preparation, Bangladesh lost all three group matches, having previously suffered 3-0 and 1-0 defeats to Malaysia and Singapore respectively.
Australia-born striker Mitchell Lee Baker scored five goals, while Rizky Ridho, Justin Hubner, Luke Vickery and Kevin Diks netted once each as Indonesia finished top of Group A with seven points.
Shahriar Emon scored Bangladesh's first goal of the tournament before England-based forward Farhaan Ali Wahid opened his international account in stoppage time.
The match proved a tense affair for the hosts, who needed to keep an eye on the simultaneous Malaysia-Singapore fixture to secure their progression to the next round.
Malaysia eventually thrashed Singapore 6-0, leaving Indonesia to advance after finishing level on seven points as well as goal difference with the Malaysians.
Indonesia took the lead in the 11th minute when Baker beat the diving Bangladesh goalkeeper with a precise finish into the far corner. The striker doubled the advantage nine minutes later to put the hosts firmly in control.
Bangladesh suffered another setback in the 27th minute when midfielder Shamit Shome was forced off through injury, with captain Sohel Rana coming on as his replacement.
Rizky Ridho extended Indonesia's lead just after the half-hour mark before Emon pulled one back for Bangladesh in the 36th minute, heading home a cross from Shuki Itofusa.
Baker completed his hat-trick in the 37th minute and added a fourth five minutes later to leave Bangladesh trailing 5-1.
Hubner struck in first-half stoppage time to make it 6-1 at the break, leaving the visitors with a daunting task in the second half.
Bangladesh showed greater resilience after the restart and managed to keep Indonesia at bay for much of the second period before Vickery found the net in the 90th minute.
Farhaan, who made his international debut against Malaysia in Bangladesh's tournament opener, then produced a flying finish to convert Rakib Hossain's cross a minute later, giving the visitors a second goal.
However, Indonesia added two more in the sixth and seventh minutes of stoppage time, with Diks scoring before Baker completed his five-goal haul to seal the emphatic victory.

item.title: Guardiola backs City after club found guilty of financial violations
item.description:
Pep Guardiola has reaffirmed his support for Manchester City after the club was found guilty of dozens of financial violations committed during his time as manager.
Guardiola, who has managed City since 2016, said he would continue to stand by the club following the publication of a report by an independent panel on Tuesday.
“I want every single Man City fan to know I am here; more than ever,” Guardiola wrote on social media Wednesday. “I am, always have been, always will be, behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran, the players, staff, Enzo and you, our unique supporters.”
“Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all,” he added in a post on X.
Guardiola's message was accompanied by photos showing him wearing a Manchester City shirt and celebrating with club chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, lifting the Champions League trophy, applauding supporters and celebrating the club's 2023 Premier League title.
During Guardiola's 10-year tenure, City won six Premier League titles, the 2023 Champions League and three FA Cups, among other trophies.
The club's alleged financial violations, which included what the league described as “sham” commercial deals, were valued at more than 900 million pounds ($1.19 billion).

item.title: Living longer, living better
item.description:
On October 1, the world observes the International Day of Older Persons 2026 under the theme, "The Age of Longevity: Rethinking Systems for Longer Lives."
For Bangladesh, this theme arrives at a defining moment. We often celebrate our youthful workforce as the country's greatest demographic dividend, yet another profound demographic transformation is unfolding alongside it: Bangladesh is quietly becoming an ageing society.
Longer lives are one of humanity's greatest achievements. They reflect better healthcare, improved nutrition, and declining mortality.
But longevity also raises an important question: Are our institutions, transport systems, healthcare services and workplaces prepared for millions of citizens who will live well beyond 60?
An ageing Bangladesh
Bangladesh officially considers all citizens aged 60 years and above as senior citizens under the National Policy on Older Persons adopted in 2013.
According to the World Health Organization, Bangladesh now has approximately 16.5 million people aged 60 and above, representing around 10% of the national population.
By 2050, this share is projected to nearly double to 19%, meaning almost one in every five Bangladeshis will be an older person.
The transition is happening remarkably fast. Bangladesh moved from around 5% elderly population in 1990 to nearly 10% by 2024, and projections indicate that the country may become an "aged society" much earlier than many expected.
This transformation is occurring while Bangladesh still enjoys a relatively large working-age population. Rather than seeing youth and ageing as competing priorities, policy-makers should recognize them as two sides of the same demographic reality.
Living longer does not automatically mean living healthier. The WHO estimates show that after turning 60, Bangladeshi women can expect to live about 20.4 more years, while men can expect around 19 years.
However, several of those additional years are often spent coping with chronic illnesses, reduced mobility, and disability.
At the same time, traditional family structures are changing. Urbanization, overseas migration, and nuclear families are weakening the informal support systems that once cared for elderly parents.
Many grandparents now shoulder childcare responsibilities while their adult children work elsewhere. Longevity, therefore, is no longer merely a family issue. It has become a national policy issue.
What Bangladesh has already achieved
The country has not remained inactive. The Old Age Allowance program, introduced in 1997, now supports around 6.1 million beneficiaries, each receiving Tk 650 per month during FY2025-26, with a budget allocation of approximately Tk 4,791 crore. Payments are increasingly delivered through mobile financial services and agent banking, improving transparency.
The government has also launched the Universal Pension Scheme, aiming to build long-term retirement security for citizens aged 18 and above. The broader vision seeks to create a sustainable pension architecture before population ageing becomes overwhelming.
Additionally, the National Healthy Ageing Strategy and Action Plan (2024-2030) has begun laying the groundwork for more age-friendly healthcare services. These are important foundations, but they are only the beginning.
Time to build an age-friendly Bangladesh
The next phase requires rethinking everyday systems rather than creating isolated welfare programs.
First , make public transport truly elderly-friendly: Reserved seating exists on paper in many buses, but enforcement remains inconsistent.
Every metro rail coach, intercity train, launch and public bus should guarantee clearly marked priority seating, easy boarding facilities, handrails, ramps and audio-visual announcements designed for older passengers. Mobility is dignity.
Second , strengthen geriatric healthcare: Every district hospital should gradually establish dedicated geriatric care units. Community clinics can expand screening for hypertension, diabetes, dementia, osteoporosis, and vision problems among older citizens. Preventive care costs far less than crisis care.
Third, design age-friendly cities: Footpaths without obstacles, safer pedestrian crossings, benches in public spaces, accessible public toilets and well-lit walkways are not luxuries. They are essential infrastructure for an ageing society.
Fourth, modernize income security: The Old Age Allowance should gradually become more adequate and more inclusive, particularly for vulnerable elderly people living alone, widows and those with disabilities. The proposed multi-tier pension system -- combining tax-financed support, contributory pensions and voluntary savings -- deserves accelerated implementation.
The untapped resource called experience
Perhaps the greatest missed opportunity lies elsewhere. Bangladesh often measures productivity only through youth employment. Yet millions of retired teachers, agricultural experts, engineers, doctors, administrators, scientists, and skilled workers possess decades of institutional knowledge.
Instead of viewing retirement as the end of public contribution -- and rather than relying solely on ad hoc contractual appointments -- Bangladesh could establish a National Senior Expertise Pool, a structured national network of retired professionals from the civil service, agriculture, health, education, engineering and other technical sectors.
By harnessing their institutional memory, field experience and policy expertise, this pool could provide advisory support to government programs.
They would not replace serving officials or occupy promotional positions. Instead, they could serve as mentors, advisers, and technical resource persons, either voluntarily or with a modest honorarium.
Experienced retirees could mentor young entrepreneurs, advise local government projects, teach technical skills, support agricultural extension, assist disaster preparedness, and volunteer in schools and community organi z ations.
Such programs would also play a part to reduce loneliness while transferring invaluable knowledge across generations.
Countries facing ageing populations increasingly promote "active ageing" rather than passive retirement. Bangladesh can adopt the philosophy without enormous financial costs.
The country already acknowledges that retirement need not mean the end of public service. In recent years, several retired secretaries and senior officials have been reappointed on contractual terms to lead important ministries, reflecting the government's recognition that institutional memory and seasoned judgment can remain valuable beyond formal retirement.
Such a model would also promote intergenerational collaboration. Bangladesh's youthful workforce remains its greatest demographic strength, yet younger officers need opportunities to learn from those who have navigated complex administrative challenges before them.
The objective should not be to prolong careers indefinitely, but to preserve valuable knowledge that would otherwise disappear on the day of retirement.
Healthy longevity is not simply about adding years to life; it is about adding value to those years. When experienced citizens continue contributing to national development in meaningful ways, ageing becomes not a burden on society but one of its greatest untapped resources.
Md Refatul Hossain is former Additional Director, DAE, and Senior Consultant, Agonochain Limited. Email: refatdae87@gmail.com .

item.title: Iran Guards hail US withdrawal from Iraq as ‘historic victory’
item.description:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Thursday welcomed the withdrawal of US forces from Iraq as a “historic victory” and called for American troops to leave the Middle East.
The Revolutionary Guards “congratulate the proud nation of Iraq, the united front of the Islamic Resistance, and the revolutionary fighters of the Islamic world on this historic victory,” the guards said in a statement carried by their official media.
On Wednesday the US-led coalition that deployed to Iraq and Syria in 2014 to fight the Islamic State (IS) group formally concluded its mission and withdrew.
IS, which seized large swathes of both countries and committed massacres and atrocities, was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group’s remnants.
“The US must leave the region and entrust the management of security to the nations themselves,” said the statement by the Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of Iran’s military.
“Two decades of occupation demonstrated that the US presence brought no security; rather, it was the very source of insecurity, terrorism, and instability in West Asia,” it added.
Baghdad and Washington agreed in 2024 to wind down the coalition’s mission, and its troops withdrew gradually from bases across the country, restricting their presence to the autonomous northern Kurdistan region.
The Iraqi government says the coalition’s withdrawal removes the excuse powerful Iran-backed militant factions have used to retain their weapons.
On Thursday, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi announced June 30 as a new deadline for armed factions to turn over their weapons to the state.

item.title: Five things to know about the Nobel Prize
item.description:
Since 1901, the Nobel Prizes have been awarded to individuals and organizations for work leading to great advances for humanity, in line with the wishes of the prizes’ founder, inventor Alfred Nobel.
The 2026 winners will be announced between October 5 and 12, starting with the Nobel Prize in Medicine on Monday from 11:30am (0930 GMT).
Here are five things to know about the prizes and their founder.
Since 1901, five Nobel Peace Prize laureates have been prevented from attending the awards ceremony in Oslo.
In 1936, German journalist and pacifist Carl von Ossietzky was detained in a Nazi concentration camp.
Myanmar opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi was under house arrest when she won the prize in 1991. Given permission by the junta to travel, she declined for fear of potentially not being able to return to her country.
In 2010, Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo was in prison. His chair remained empty, where the prize was placed.
In 2022, Belarusian human rights campaigner Ales Bialiatski was in jail. He was represented by his wife Natalia Pinchuk.
In 2023, Iranian activist Narges Mohammadi was held in Iran’s Evin prison when the prize was awarded.
In 2014, 17-year-old Pakistani human rights activist Malala Yousafzai became the youngest winner of a Nobel Prize.
Another unusually young laureate was Australia’s Lawrence Bragg, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics jointly with his father in 1915 when he was 25, for work carried out at the age of 21.
Iraqi Nadia Murad was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize at the age of 25 in 2018 for her efforts on behalf of the Yazidi minority.
In contrast, American John Goodenough was the oldest to become a Nobel laureate. He won the Prize in Chemistry in 2019 at the age of 97 for his work on the lithium-ion batteries that power smartphones and electric cars.
The year before, his compatriot Arthur Ashkin was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics at the age of 96.
Since 1974, the statutes of the Nobel Foundation stipulate that the prize may not be given posthumously.
But the prize may still be awarded if the recipient dies between the time of the announcement in October and the formal prize ceremony in December.
Before the change, only two people had won a Nobel posthumously.
One was Dag Hammarskjold, the Swedish secretary-general of the United Nations, who died in a plane crash in 1961 but was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize later the same year.
And in 1931, the Nobel Literature Prize was awarded posthumously to another Swede, poet Erik Axel Karlfeldt.
In 2011, the committee for the Nobel Prize in Medicine selected Ralph Steinman of Canada, unaware that he had passed away just three days before the announcement.
The foundation nevertheless gave him the award.
Only 68 of the 633 Nobel prizes awarded since 1901 have been given to women, representing about 10%, though the share has been steadily increasing since the early 2020s.
The science fields have the lowest representation of women laureates. The various committees that award the prizes have repeatedly refused to introduce quotas, instead encouraging nominations of women scientists.
Only five women have won a Nobel physics prize out of a total of 230 laureates in the discipline, three out of 99 economics laureates, eight out of 200 chemistry laureates, and 14 out of 232 medicine laureates.
Marie Curie was the first woman laureate in 1903 and she is to this day the only woman to have received two Nobel prizes, first for physics in 1903 and then in 1911 in chemistry.
Nobel went down in history as the inventor of dynamite but he also loved English poetry and was an admirer of Percy Bysshe Shelley and Byron.
He wrote poetry himself his entire life, sometimes in his native Swedish but mostly in English.
In a letter to a friend, he wrote: “I have not the slightest pretension to call my verses poetry; I write now and then for no other purpose than to relieve depression, or to improve my English.”
In 1862, at the age of 29 and questioning his literary talent, he sent a letter in French to a young woman that said: “Physics is my field, not writing.”
In 1896, the year of his death, he wrote a scandalous tragedy in four acts titled “Nemesis,” inspired by Shelley’s play “The Cenci” about a woman in 16th-century Rome who murders her incestuous father.

item.title: Are the Houthis winning against Saudi Arabia?
item.description:
Last week, some students in Saudi Arabia were told they should stay at home and attend classes online, due to continued threats from attacks by the Houthi group in neighboring Yemen. But the very next day, they were given the all-clear and allowed to return to school in person.
The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen seems to have become part of everyday life in Saudi Arabia. After a period of comparative calm, the Houthis have been ramping up attacks on the country, starting July, and have fired many missiles and drones over the border.
Over recent weeks, the Houthi militia have also pushed further into Yemen, taking more control of the Yemeni coast and several islands in the Red Sea. This means they can oversee maritime traffic in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The renewed Houthi attacks endanger Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia’s ambitious project to move the kingdom away from its dependence on oil revenues, which was conceived by Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. To make Vision 2030 a reality, Saudi Arabia needs stability — but right now, the outlook is moving in the opposite direction.
“The escalation in Yemen is drawing the Saudis deeper into the regional war, a war that Saudi Arabia actually wanted to prevent,” said Marcus Schneider, who heads the Friedrich Ebert Foundation’s Regional Peace and Security Project in the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure is particularly vulnerable to Houthi attacks, which have already disrupted the so-called East-West pipeline, which runs for over 1,200 kilometers. It was being used to transport oil after other routes, such as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, became precarious due to fighting between the United States, Israel and Iran.
Houthi attacks disabled the pipeline although reports from a week ago suggest it is being used again. And thanks to the Houthis, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which means “gate of tears” in English — is also coming under pressure.
Andrew Leber, a nonresident scholar in the Middle East program of the US think tank, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, calls it a “one-two punch of pipeline attacks and Red Sea seizures.” In fact, it may send the Saudis back to the Strait of Hormuz to try to ship their oil, even though that route is still heavily restricted.
It is unlikely that Saudi ally, the US, is going to send help. Washington has said it will support the Saudis with intelligence and reconnaissance, but President Donald Trump appears reluctant to get involved in a direct military campaign against the Houthis.
According to a US-based think tank, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, this may partially be because the it is feeling the strain of its ongoing campaign against Iran.
“The US military is reportedly facing serious challenges, including shortages of some sophisticated interceptors,” the CSIS wrote in a commentary last week.
The US Council on Foreign Relations, or CFR, has also written about dwindling stocks of Patriot and interceptor missiles, as well as cruise missiles.
So the risk of opening another front in its war with Iran, in Yemen, is not a welcome prospect for the US.
As it is, US airstrikes are unlikely to resolve the Houthi problem anyway. The CFR writes that to defuse the Houthi threat, a large, coordinated ground operation is needed, especially if forces want to push the Yemeni militia back out of the areas they recently took around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Saudi Arabia is not too enthusiastic about this either. Despite help from the US and neighboring United Arab Emirates, a Saudi coalition that fought against the Houthis between 2015 and 2022 failed to achieve any kind of decisive victory. It also demonstrated the limits of Saudi military power.
There’s clear military asymmetry. Saudi Arabia possesses modern weapons and spends enormous sums on its armed forces. But the Houthis don’t need to win a conventional war. It is enough for them to use missiles and drones to threaten infrastructure and disrupt shipping.
“The Houthis are well-established in Yemen and can withstand considerable blows,” Schneider told DW. “Saudi Arabia, on the other hand, needs stability above all for its 2030 economic vision. And this is currently further away than ever.”
Since early 2024, through what is known as Operation Aspides, Europe has been protecting international shipping in the Red Sea. Italy has recently said it intends to secure passage for its own merchant ships with its navy. And a few days ago France said it would send soldiers, radar systems and air defense to the Saudis in order to protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the terminus of the East-West pipeline.
Still, these European initiatives are unlikely to bring about any sort of strategic shift in Yemen. And experts argue Europe is unwilling to accept the political and military cost of a protracted war there.
“The fact that France has now announced it will provide concrete military assistance has been received very positively in Riyadh,” Schneider explained. “But still the question remains as to whether this can fundamentally alter the military balance.”
The recently formed mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey, known as the Mecca alliance, also has its limits. The military leaders of all three countries have consulted with one another over recent Houthis attacks but Turkey and Pakistan are also reluctant to be drawn into a conflict that would see them confronting Iran directly.
All this means that diplomatic overtures will likely become more important again.
In a previous interview with DW, Abdulghani al-Iryani of the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies noted that the Houthis do actually have an interest in relations with Saudi Arabia.
“Yemen is completely economically dependent on Saudi Arabia, both as a source of humanitarian aid and as a labor market for Yemeni migrant workers,” al-Iryani said.
In recent years, Saudi Arabia has tried to curb the Houthis’ influence through diplomacy and by uniting divided Yemeni government forces. However the militia’s current advance seems to demonstrate the limitations of this strategy.

item.title: Woman in hospital after Tennessee’s second failed execution in 2026
item.description:
A Tennessee woman convicted of murder survived two lethal injection doses and was hospitalized on Thursday, her lawyers said, marking the state’s second failed execution in months and prompting it to halt capital punishment this year.
Hours earlier on Wednesday the Supreme Court cleared the way for Christa Pike, 50, to become the first woman to be executed in the southern US state of Tennessee in 200 years -- but the attempt failed.
“This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, told the New York Times. “There is no precedent.”
The Tennessee Department of Correction said that it “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol,” adding that Pike was subsequently taken to an “off-site medical facility.”
Her attorneys said she was transported to a nearby hospital, adding they have not been informed as to her condition.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” the attorneys said in a statement.
Tennessee halted the execution by lethal injection of Tony Carruthers in May after medical staff were unable to tap a vein.
Governor Bill Lee called for a “comprehensive, third-party review” after Pike’s failed execution.
“The remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year,” Lee said -- apparently referencing the execution of convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton scheduled for December 3.
Pike was scheduled for execution at 10:00 am (1500 GMT) at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, where witnesses including journalists were present for the administration of the injections.
Kim Chandler, a media witness with Associated Press, told CBS News that “Pike appeared notably awake as the execution began.”
After the blinds of the execution chamber closed for the final time, Pike “could be heard loudly snoring, clearly very alive in the chamber until media witnesses were told to leave the area,” Chandler said.
During a livestream, an ambulance with its lights flashing could be seen leaving the site of the execution. It was unclear if it was transporting Pike.
The execution procedure went ahead hours after the US Supreme Court ruled that it could proceed, with liberal justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson all dissenting.
“The Court’s decision... unnecessarily prevents that (lower) court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim,” the dissenting justices wrote.
“Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the State to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts.”
The case has sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer’s body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike’s lawyers argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing.
“She was 18 when she committed her crime, and she was deeply mentally ill,” they wrote in a clemency petition to Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, who said he would not intervene.
The US Supreme Court had rejected Tuesday an application for a stay of execution, which argued that Pike’s history as a victim of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause “needless suffering.”
Independent UN rights experts have urged the US government and Tennessee authorities to “immediately halt” the execution and commute her death sentence.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

item.title: IUBAT ranks joint second in Bangladesh in THE World University Rankings 2027
item.description:
The International University of Business Agriculture and Technology (IUBAT) has been ranked joint second among universities in Bangladesh in the Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings 2027, published by the UK-based higher education magazine. Globally, the university is placed in the 1001–1200 band.
THE published the rankings on its official website on Wednesday, September 30. This year’s edition assessed 2,297 universities from 118 countries.
The other universities sharing the joint second position in Bangladesh are Bangladesh Agricultural University (BAU), Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET), BRAC University, Gazipur Agricultural University (GAU), Jessore University of Science and Technology (JUST), the University of Dhaka (DU) and the University of Rajshahi (RU).
The THE World University Rankings are among the most widely recognized university rankings globally. Institutions are assessed on five core pillars: teaching, research environment, research quality including citations, international outlook and industry engagement.
The student-to-staff ratio and the proportion of international students are also part of the evaluation.
According to the university, the ranking reflects IUBAT’s progress in academic quality, research activity and global engagement. Its emphasis on applied education, international collaboration, research and community engagement has contributed to its position in the global rankings.
Commenting on the achievement, IUBAT Treasurer Professor Selina Nargis said: “Being ranked joint second in Bangladesh in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings is a recognition of the tireless hard work and dedication of every member of the IUBAT family.
“This success has come through the collective efforts of our faculty, students, staff and alumni. Since our founding as the country’s first private university, we have prioritized quality education, applied research and international collaboration.
“This global recognition shows that we are on the right path. In the coming days, we will continue working to expand our research, strengthen our links with industry and prepare our students to be globally competent.
“Our goal is to take IUBAT to even greater heights as a world-class institution.”
The university authority expressed gratitude to faculty, students, staff, alumni and everyone involved in the achievement, and reaffirmed its commitment to academic excellence, innovation and building a world-class institution.
The International University of Business Agriculture and Technology was founded in 1991 by academic Professor Dr M Alimullah Miyan as the first private university in Bangladesh.
Located on a green campus in Uttara, Dhaka, the university offers undergraduate and postgraduate programs in business administration, agriculture, engineering, computer science, nursing and other disciplines.
IUBAT’s mission is to produce skilled, ethical and globally competent graduates.

item.title: ‘Game of Thrones: Aegon’s Conquest’ sets 2029 release date
item.description:
The “Game of Thrones” universe is heading to the big screen with “Game of Thrones: Aegon’s Conquest”, scheduled to hit cinemas on June 6, 2029.
Warner Bros has announced the theatrical release date, with Owen Harris attached to direct and Beau W illimon writing the screenplay.
Plot details remain under wraps, but the film is expected to follow Aegon I Targaryen, also known as Aegon the Conqueror, and his campaign to conquer and unite the Seven Kingdoms.
Set roughly 300 years before the events of the original “Game of Thrones”, the film will explore the establishment of the Targaryen dynasty in Westeros. No casting has yet been announced for the role of Aegon.
Harris, who directed three episodes of “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms”, is also an executive producer on the series. His other television credits include “Black Mirror”, “The Twilight Zone” and “Brave New World”.
Willimon is best known as the creator and showrunner of “House of Cards” and for his work on “Andor”.
The original “Game of Thrones”, based on George RR Martin’s “A Song of Ice and Fire” novels, ran for eight seasons from 2011 to 2019.
The franchise has since expanded with prequel projects including “House of the Dragon” and “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms”.
